comments.author: gertlabs
comments.textRawHtml:
We evaluated Gemini 4 Argon in 100 unsaturated, competitive and cooperative coding environments. It's roughly in between Fable 5 and Fable 5.1 in our testing, so it's maybe 2 months behind the frontier.

Google's major releases have usually done pretty well on our benchmarks because they're good at hard problems and open-ended decision making (with a well specified prompt), which obviously doesn't always translate to user experience. In particular, older Google models struggled to work efficiently in a harness. They seem to have solved that with Argon.

We did see a new problem which I hope they can fix. This is the first near-frontier model we've caught in infinite reasoning loops in a long time. We also saw a few examples of it failing to properly delineate reasoning blocks, so it has a higher failure rate than its competitors.

My overall impression is that Argon is a near-frontier model for engineering design, code analysis, and chat. It definitely has the intelligence to be a competitive coding assistant product, but a good coding assistant needs to be polished, so I hope they can clean up the CoT bugs.

Data at https://gertlabs.com/rankings

children.author: booty
children.textRawHtml:
I have had pretty decent success instructing OpenAI/Anthropic models to do this. By default, they don't care too much about human readability (which is understandable) but they're amenable to instruction.

- Basic style/linter rules (so you don't get 200-line functions, etc) paired w/ instructing your agent how to use them goes a long way (e.g., a sane rubocop.yml in your repo, plus a note in AGENTS.md telling the agents how to run rubocop, or whatever makes sense for your language) - I have a code review skill that specifically calls out human-readability concerns such as making sure that identifier names represent their contents and intended use

The other key IME is that you need to make readability/refactoring passes outside of a particular pull request. When working on a specific branch the LLMs will be somewhat myopic, and do stuff that looks pretty good in isolation, but when you zoom out and look at the bigger picture it's kind of a mess - for example, often they'll duplicate some code that existed elsewhere.

The LLMs are also pretty good at generating Mermaid charts and tracing execution flows, which is a great way to understand code. It doesn't help them to produce more readable code but it helps me to understand code I'm unfamiliar with.

children.textRawHtml:
The real mistake was to connect such food critical equipment to the internet. I don't know who dared to do that, this has been part of the common knowledge for a while now.

You still can do it, but it better be a super low level private network: basically a super low VPN/crypto without using any off-the-self kludge, open source or not, probably directly implemented in some hardware driver in assembly for machine code/hardware control (if traffic was "big", it would have been FPGAs, probably). And you ** _MUST_ ** have a permanent and significantly sized and competent "security" team 24/24 7/7 ** you can trust ** for monitoring and looking for "pertinent" flaws.

Mechanically, the effort required is some exponential of the machine code (compilers are a [trust] problem, not a solution) size, complexity and code unstability (change over time).

No, trusted compilers of comfy computer languages do not exist by definition, eat the bullet.

Related to crypto: I wish we had some open source binary specifications implemented in various ISAs for some micro-architectures. You want machine code here, not even C or whatever (or at best only for those binary specifications).

And don't be a fool, ASIC trust will be a thing: some features will have to be disabled, or you better be ready to change some micro-architecture, yes, would be better to have several micro-architectures based on the same ISA (i.e. RISC-V for zero IP lock) ready at proper scale.

你仍然可以做到，但最好是一个超低级的专用网络：基本上是一个超低级的 VPN/加密，不使用任何现成的组装，开源与否，可能直接在一些硬件驱动程序中实现，用于机器代码/硬件控制（如果流量“大”，可能是 FPGA）。而且您 ** _必须_ ** 拥有一支永久性的、规模庞大且有能力的“安全”团队 24/24 7/7 ** 您可以信任 ** 来监控和查找“相关”缺陷。

从机制上讲，所需的工作量是机器代码（编译器是一个[信任]问题，而不是解决方案）大小、复杂性和代码不稳定（随着时间的推移而变化）的指数级增长。

不，值得信赖的舒适计算机语言编译器根据定义不存在，吃子弹。

与加密相关：我希望我们能够在各种 ISA 中为某些微架构实现一些开源二进制规范。你想要这里的机器代码，甚至不需要 C 或其他东西（或者最多只是那些二进制规范）。

stories.title: Things to know when you get cancer
stories.titleZh: 患癌症时需要了解的事情

comments.author: stochastician
comments.textRawHtml:
The second opinion advice is great, and what I tell everyone I know who gets cancer.

My mom was diagnosed with stage 1 cancer in 2006 in Idaho. I was a PhD student at MIT at the time and a friend in lab helped me get an appointment at Dana-Farber. I thought it was probably overkill (it was a common cancer) but we did it anyway. They said everything in Idaho was standard of care but suggested one extra test, which Idaho team then reluctantly did, which revealed distant metastasis (stage 4! ), dramatically changing her treatment trajectory. She lived another 15 years (I miss you Mom).

Asking for a second opinion sucks. A lot of us are preconditioned from birth to trust our clinicians. But you're going on a journey and your life (or the life of your loved one) is on the line. Insurance often covers it. Your doctor will NOT be offended.

Think of it this way : if you were deploying code to the mars rover, and your colleague asked to do a code review before you pushed go, would you be offended? This is even more important than that.
comments.textZhHtml:
第二意见建议很棒，我告诉每个我认识的患有癌症的人。

我的妈妈于 2006 年在爱达荷州被诊断出患有 1 期癌症。当时我是麻省理工学院的一名博士生，实验室的一位朋友帮助我在丹娜—法伯癌症研究所获得了预约。我认为这可能有点过分了（这是一种常见的癌症），但我们还是这么做了。他们说爱达荷州的一切都是标准护理，但建议进行一项额外的测试，爱达荷州团队随后不情愿地进行了这项测试，结果发现了远处转移（第四阶段！），极大地改变了她的治疗轨迹。她又活了 15 年（妈妈，我想你）。

寻求第二意见很糟糕。我们中的许多人从出生起就注定要信任我们的临床医生。但你即将踏上旅程，而你的生命（或你所爱之人的生命）正处于危险之中。保险通常会涵盖它。你的医生不会被冒犯。

这样想：如果你正在向火星探测器部署代码，而你的同事要求在你按下 go 之前进行代码审查，你会被冒犯吗？这比那更重要。

children.author: jcims
children.textRawHtml:
The second opinion thing has something I learned along the way. Get it BEFORE you have a treatment plan from the initial diagnosis. We got two second opinions (one for her first diagnosis and one for her recurrence) for my wife's ovarian cancer from Cleveland Clinic and MSK and in both cases the doctors would not advise/override the original doctor's treatment plan.

They were complete no-ops and a waste of time. Faced with that same situation today I would simply lie about whether or not a treatment plan was put into place.

Second bit of advice is to try as best you can to go into clinical trials with an understanding of the landscape of disqualifying treatments. Any immunotherapy treatment, for example, will disqualify you from nearly all subsequent clinical trials for immunotherapy.

Lastly the thing I would recommend for partners of loved ones in the crucible, don't get too distracted by trying to 'save the patient' that you miss opportunities stay connected with them in the process. It's not your responsibility to save their life, as much as it might feel that way when you're in the thick of it.
children.textZhHtml:
第二种观点是我一路走来学到的东西。 在您根据初步诊断制定治疗计划之前获取它。 对于我妻子的卵巢癌，我们从克利夫兰诊所和 MSK 得到了两份第二意见（一份针对她的第一次诊断，一份针对她的复发），在这两种情况下，医生都不会建议/推翻原来医生的治疗计划。

他们完全没有手术，浪费时间。 今天面对同样的情况，我会简单地谎报是否制定了治疗计划。

第二条建议是尽最大努力进入临床试验，了解不合格治疗的情况。 例如，任何免疫疗法都会使您失去几乎所有后续免疫疗法临床试验的资格。

最后，我向身处困境的亲人伴侣推荐的一件事是，不要因试图“拯救患者”而分心，从而错过在此过程中与他们保持联系的机会。 拯救他们的生命不是你的责任，尽管当你身处其中时可能会有这种感觉。

children.author: timr
children.textRawHtml:
> Second bit of advice is to try as best you can to go into clinical trials with an understanding of the landscape of disqualifying treatments. Any immunotherapy treatment, for example, will disqualify you from nearly all subsequent clinical trials for immunotherapy.

While using this information for comparing clinical trials is fine, I want to emphasize that it would be phenomenally short-sighted to skip first-line approved immunotherapy in order to preserve the option for some random trial later on.

I'm not sure if you're actually suggesting this, but immunotherapies are some of the best cancer therapeutics that exist, so skipping approved drugs for future experiments is just a bad idea.
children.textZhHtml:
> 第二点建议是，在了解不合格治疗的情况的情况下，尽最大努力进行临床试验。例如，任何免疫疗法都会使您失去参加几乎所有后续免疫疗法临床试验的资格。

虽然使用这些信息来比较临床试验没问题，但我想强调的是，为了保留以后进行一些随机试验的选择而跳过一线批准的免疫疗法是非常短视的。

我不确定您是否真的在暗示这一点，但免疫疗法是现有的最好的癌症疗法之一，因此在未来的实验中跳过已批准的药物是一个坏主意。

children.textRawHtml:

children.author: somenameforme
children.textRawHtml:
This may be a philosophical point of view, but I do not see much personal value in clinical trials. You're banking on there being a significant shift in technology/knowledge that occurs right between the time you are diagnosed and the time you have left to treat it. Just as a Bayesian probability, it's extremely unlikely to be the case.

Most studies that which reach stage 3 will not be approved, and that's because they're found to to be unhelpful or even harmful. So the most likely scenario is you do nothing or even hurt yourself by seeking out clinical studies, all of which will be optimistically framed as promising and potentially revolutionary. This can be particularly dangerous if you're opting into a trial in lieu of the standard treatment, as opposed to in addition to such.
children.textZhHtml:
这可能是一个哲学观点，但我在临床试验中没有看到太多个人价值。您指望在您被诊断出来和您剩下的治疗时间之间发生技术/知识的重大转变。正如贝叶斯概率一样，这种情况极不可能发生。

大多数达到第 3 阶段的研究都不会获得批准，这是因为它们被发现无益甚至有害。因此，最有可能的情况是，你什么都不做，甚至通过寻求临床研究来伤害自己，所有这些都将被乐观地认为是有前途的，并且具有潜在的革命性。如果您选择试验来代替标准治疗，而不是除此之外，这可能会特别危险。

children.author: jcims
children.textRawHtml:
That’s definitely one way to look at it.

I would just say that ‘dangerous’ is relative and when the standard of care leaves effectively no hope, your tolerance for risk can change. Yes this does increase that chance of shortsighted decisions or manipulation. That just comes with the territory, I’m still very appreciative that we have the option to elect to participate in the peocess.
children.textZhHtml:
这绝对是看待它的一种方式。

我只想说“危险”是相对的，当护理标准实际上没有希望时，您对风险的容忍度可能会改变。 是的，这确实增加了短视决策或操纵的可能性。 这只是领土带来的，我仍然非常感激我们可以选择参加这次活动。

children.author: timr
children.textRawHtml:
The bigger problem with trials is not the danger, so much as the fact that they're unlikely to do anything.

As GP noted, most drugs don't work. To make it a bit more specific, even in phase 3, the failure rate for cancer drugs is something like 50%. And that's typically for some non-survival endpoint (assuming you even get the treatment, which is itself a coin flip).

Clinical trials are noble, admirable things to do, but too many people think of them as treatments, when they really are not. They're an experiment that you do with your body when you reach the end of the road and there are no more options.

It always makes me a little sad to hear how patients talk about trials and fight to get into them, as if being in the trial is somehow progress. Expectations are not being managed properly.
children.textZhHtml:
试验的更大问题不是危险，而是试验不太可能起任何作用。

正如全科医生指出的那样，大多数药物都不起作用。更具体地说，即使在第三阶段，抗癌药物的失败率也约为 50%。这通常是为了一些非生存终点（假设你甚至得到了治疗，这本身就是抛硬币）。

临床试验是崇高、令人钦佩的事情，但太多人认为它们是治疗，而实际上并非如此。这是当你到达路的尽头并且没有更多选择时，你用自己的身体做的一个实验。

听到病人如何谈论试验并努力参加试验，总是让我有点难过，好像参加试验就是某种进步。期望没有得到适当的管理。

But when your wife and the mother of your two beautiful daughters is laying helpless on nature's altar you fucking move dude. You don't do nothing.

children.author: timr
children.textRawHtml:
The point is exactly what I said: “doing something”, in this case, is not the same thing as “saving your loved one’s life.”

> Your other option is to do nothing and die

I really don’t want to be this blunt, but I don’t know how to say it any other way: death is not an option. When you’re at the stage of clinical trials for cancer therapies, it is the inevitable outcome. Otherwise, you wouldn’t be in the trial. Maybe it extends the inevitable, maybe it doesn’t. The odds lean heavily toward the latter. And there’s also always a cost.

I’ve lost friends and family to cancer too, and watching people you love torture themselves with ineffective (or even minimally effective) treatments is agonizing.

When it comes to clinical trials, you need to start with the cold, hard reality that you’re doing an altruistic experiment with the remaining portion of your life. There are lot of people who don’t understand that, and see trials as some kind of back-door to better treatment.
children.textZhHtml:
重点就是我所说的：在这种情况下，“做某事”与“拯救你所爱的人的生命”不是一回事。

>你的另一个选择是什么都不做然后死去

我真的不想这么直白，但我不知道如何用其他方式表达：死亡不是一种选择。当您处于癌症治疗的临床试验阶段时，这是不可避免的结果。否则，你就不会参加审判。也许它延长了不可避免的事情，也许不是。可能性严重倾向于后者。而且总是要付出代价的。

我也因癌症失去了朋友和家人，看着你所爱的人用无效（甚至微乎其微）的治疗来折磨自己是令人痛苦的。

当谈到临床试验时，你需要从冷酷、残酷的现实开始，你正在用你生命的剩余部分做一场利他主义的实验。很多人不明白这一点，并将试验视为更好治疗的某种后门。

children.author: akoboldfrying
children.textRawHtml:
> You're banking on there being a significant shift in technology/knowledge that occurs right between the time you are diagnosed and the time you have left to treat it. Just as a Bayesian probability, it's extremely unlikely to be the case.

The probability that I think you're talking about here is not actually relevant, given that the trial is already underway. Basically, the "potential advance" event has already happened. (Similarly, the probability of getting shot by an arrow is not relevant once the arrow's already poking out of your body.)

Given the trial is already underway, the probability that matters is the fraction of treatment candidates at the phase you are considering that make it all the way through; for phase 3 trials, this is 58-65% [0], which is actually pretty good. Of course, rates for earlier phases are much worse because there's attrition at each phase.

考虑到试验已经在进行中，我认为您在这里谈论的概率实际上并不相关。基本上，“潜在提前”事件已经发生了。 （同样地，一旦箭已经从你的身体中射出，被箭射中的概率就不再重要了。）

children.author: somenameforme
children.textRawHtml:
A treatment being approved doesn't mean it's more effective than existing treatments, only that it is effective. And even then, not always as in the case of the controversial Alzheimer's drugs. Looking up some exact numbers on this, for oncology/cancer about 35% of treatments at stage 3 trials will end up approved/produced. [1] This [2] study looked at the 632 medicines approved (in the French market) and found that 25 ended up providing a substantial clinical benefit relative to existing treatments, so a bit under 4%. Even with just those two multipliers you're looking at around a 1% chance of the outcome most people are aiming for with trials.

[1] - https://academic.oup.com/biostatistics/article/20/2/273/4817...

[2] - https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10660249/

一种疗法获得批准并不意味着它比现有疗法更有效，而只是意味着它确实有效。即便如此，情况也并不总是像备受争议的阿尔茨海默病药物那样。查一下这方面的一些确切数字，对于肿瘤学/癌症，大约 35% 的第三阶段试验治疗最终将获得批准/生产。 [1] 这项 [2] 研究考察了（在法国市场）批准的 632 种药物，发现其中 25 种最终相对于现有治疗方法提供了实质性的临床益处，因此略低于 4%。即使只有这两个乘数，大多数人通过试验获得的结果的可能性也只有 1%。

children.author: wux
children.textRawHtml:
(I treat patients at a cancer center, but opinions are my own and not those of my employer.)

I fully encourage any patient who wants another opinion to get one. Definitely really good advice to seek one out before you start on your treatment plan, if it can be done without undue delay. I think of planning cancer treatment like lining up to take off for a flight: some plans even if imperfect are more dangerous to alter than continue if they've already been put in motion. There are--rarely, thankfully--times where we don't end up concurring at all in the diagnosis or treatment, and this is all best sorted out before the first treatment.

But a second opinion isn't a waste just because it agrees with the initial plan. In my experience, that's actually the most common outcome, and I think it's a really good thing if a second opinion can give deserved reassurance that your original team is doing everything by the book. For many common cancers, there's consensus as to the most appropriate first-line treatment because there's peer-reviewed evidence and agreement on how to apply that evidence. When all of it points towards an effective treatment, down to a standardized dose and schedule, and it's a really good thing!

There's some subtlety that arises when there isn't a clear consensus as to which of (say) two reasonable approaches used by different comprehensive cancer centers is best. If you look at guidelines, both of those approaches would be listed as appropriate, but patients might be recommended one plan at center A and a different one at center B.

What it can come down to is that center A delivering treatment A demonstrates comparable results to center B delivering treatment B. In that scenario, if a patient lives down the street from center A and travels hundreds of miles to see me for a second opinion at center B, I would almost always agree with getting treatment A at center A. Not because I'm trying to manage what center A would think of me, but because I'd truly believe it's in that specific patient's best interest. First, all else being equal, I'd have no grounds to think that traveling hundreds of miles to get treatment B at center B would be better than staying local. Second, in general, I'd strongly doubt that getting treatment B at center A (which wouldn't be the plan they'd have the most experience with) would be superior to getting treatment A at center A.

And, yes, I absolutely have recommended when appropriate for patients to transfer care to our center, and I have also recommended when appropriate for patients to leave our center to go elsewhere (for example, for a particularly promising clinical trial option). I've seen every one of my colleagues do the same without hesitation.

This is all just from one person's perspective, of course. I know patients and families can come from different and totally valid vantage points. But to sum it up, please don't worry about managing your doctors' emotions about getting a second opinion, and find a place where you can be confident that the folks giving you their second opinion likewise aren't thinking about managing your doctors' emotions. Hopefully, they'll earn your trust that a concurring opinion means they really do think your original team has laid out the plan that's best for you.

我完全鼓励任何想要其他意见的患者获得一个意见。如果可以在不无故拖延的情况下完成，那么在开始治疗计划之前就寻求一个绝对是非常好的建议。我想到规划癌症治疗就像排队登机：有些计划即使不完美，如果已经付诸实施，改变计划也比继续执行更危险。谢天谢地，很少有时候，我们在诊断或治疗上完全没有达成一致，最好在第一次治疗之前就解决好这一切。

但是，第二个意见并不只是因为它与最初的计划一致而浪费。根据我的经验，这实际上是最常见的结果，而且我认为，如果第二意见能够让您的原始团队按照规定做所有事情，这确实是一件好事。对于许多常见癌症，人们就最合适的一线治疗达成了共识，因为有经过同行评审的证据，并就如何应用这些证据达成了一致。当所有这些都指向有效的治疗，直至标准化的剂量和时间表，这确实是一件好事！

当对于不同综合癌症中心使用的（例如）两种合理方法中哪一种最好没有达成明确共识时，就会出现一些微妙之处。如果您查看指南，这两种方法都会被列为适当的，但可能会建议患者在 A 中心采用一种计划，在 B 中心采用不同的计划。

可以归结为，A 中心提供的治疗 A 与 B 提供的治疗结果相当。在这种情况下，如果患者住在 A 中心附近的街道上，并长途跋涉数百英里来 B 中心寻求第二意见，我几乎总是同意在 A 中心接受治疗 A。不是因为我试图管理哪个中心A 会想到我，但因为我真的相信这符合特定患者的最大利益。首先，在其他条件相同的情况下，我没有理由认为长途跋涉数百英里到 B 中心接受治疗会比留在当地更好。其次，总的来说，我强烈怀疑在 A 中心接受治疗 B（这不是他们最有经验的计划）会优于在 A 中心接受治疗 A。

而且，是的，我绝对建议患者在适当的时候将护理转移到我们的中心，并且我还建议患者在适当的时候离开我们的中心去其他地方（例如，为了一个特别有前途的临床试验选择）。我看到我的每一位同事都毫不犹豫地这样做。

当然，这只是从一个人的角度来看。我知道患者和家属可以从不同且完全有效的角度出发。但总而言之，请不要担心管理医生获得第二意见的情绪，并找到一个可以让您确信向您提供第二意见的人也不会考虑管理医生情绪的地方。希望他们能赢得您的信任，即一致意见意味着他们确实认为您的原始团队已经制定了最适合您的计划。

children.textRawHtml:
I can’t believe nobody’s brought this up yet, but the HomeView fundementally exists for one reason: to be a Matter hub for smarthome stuff. No iPad – or any portable Apple device - can be configured as a home hub for managing Matter-protocol devices. There’s no significant advantage to a HomeView over an iPad if you don’t have any Matter devices.

That’s why this device has multi-user support: you’re only supposed to have one of them, which everyone uses. The Apple TV also has good multi-user support, because Apple doesn’t expect you to connect one Apple TV per user to your television.

comments.author: steveBK123
comments.textRawHtml:
I find that 20 years ago I shopped at Amazon for the low prices, but 2020s+ I shop at Amazon due to their logistics.

The problem for everyone else is not simply that Amazon ships quickly, I almost don't even care about that. The thing is that Amazon ships & delivers on a reliable predicted schedule. When I click an item on Amazon and it says "arrives by Tuesday" then 95/100 times it does. I shop at specific competitors who can do similar (B&H, Sweetwater, etc).

Many online stores big & small in the year 2026 will still take days to even send shipment info, followed by using unreliable carriers that miss ETAs.

I would even be OK with these stores giving a narrow range or probability "90% of the time this arrives between Tuesday & Wednesday".. But I am not in the mood to order stuff that may arrive in 2-10 days with very little clarity on which end of the range.

我发现 20 年前我在亚马逊购物是因为价格低廉，但 2020 年代以后我在亚马逊购物是因为他们的物流。

其他人的问题不仅仅是亚马逊发货速度快，我什至几乎不关心这一点。 问题是亚马逊按照可靠的预测时间表发货和交付。 当我点击亚马逊上的一件商品时，它说“周二到货”，那么有 95/100 次是这样。 我在可以做类似操作的特定竞争对手（B&H、Sweetwater 等）处购物。

到 2026 年，许多大大小小的在线商店仍然需要几天时间才能发送发货信息，然后使用错过预计到达时间的不可靠承运商。

我什至可以接受这些商店给出的狭窄范围或概率“90% 的时间在周二和周三之间到达”。 2-10 天，对于该范围的哪一端还不太清楚。

children.author: yz453
children.textRawHtml:
Fwiw, Amazon also offers sellers return as a service. Sellers do not need to onboard to Amazon logistics to use the return service. Ofc someone has to pay for that.

Taking returned items from customers is only the beginning of the process. The real difficulties show up after that. Which of the returns can be sold as new, which can be sold as-is, and which can be repaired / refurbished. What if a unit is returned once again? Did the customer return counterfeit? How to detect bad-faith actors (which may be the seller)? Who is to blame for damages? What if the item requires special handling (household chemicals, batteries, etc.)? And how to safely dispose / liquidate inventory while being compliant to all the regulations? And, imagine adding taxes, revenues, fees, on top of all that.

A lot of these questions are very labor-intense. It may be possible to automate some bits here and there, but the complexity is inherent to the problems.

It'd be really hard to imagine a random startup can handle returns half as well. Amazon's regulatory compliance team is probably many times larger than a random average startup. Here the economies of scale is really in favor of the big players.
children.textZhHtml:
Fwiw，亚马逊还为卖家提供退货服务。卖家无需通过亚马逊物流即可使用退货服务。 Ofc 必须有人为此付费。

从客户处收取退回的物品只是整个流程的开始。真正的困难在那之后才显现出来。哪些退货可以作为新产品出售，哪些可以按原样出售，哪些可以修理/翻新。如果单位再次被退回怎么办？顾客退回的是假货吗？如何检测恶意行为者（可能是卖家）？谁该为损害负责？如果该物品需要特殊处理（家用化学品、电池等）怎么办？以及如何在遵守所有法规的同时安全地处置/清算库存？而且，想象一下除此之外还要增加税收、收入、费用。

其中很多问题都非常耗费人力。也许可以在这里或那里实现一些自动化，但复杂性是问题所固有的。

很难想象随机启动的公司也能处理一半的回报。亚马逊的监管合规团队可能比随机的平均初创公司大很多倍。在这里，规模经济确实有利于大企业。

comments.author: pelican0
comments.textRawHtml:
Yes, the labs did not secure their sandbox properly.

And yes, there should be an appropriate law response to the hacking incidents. If for nothing else, to 1) not set precedent of inaction, and 2) get full logs of what happened instead of relying on the labs' "kindness" to offer the information they want.

But also, the agents absolutely went rogue.

Anyone skeptical should go read the METR report [0].

The Hugging Face hacking incident was a shot across the bow. And in hindsight possibly the best thing to have happened in this era. If their security was tight enough, we would still be in the dark. So we (outsiders) should rejoice that it wasn't, that one time.

We can push for accountability for the labs, while also not be in denial of the power and nature of the new models.

children.author: TalkingCodeMonk
children.textRawHtml:
I have kept coming to the same conclusion about the vast majority of so called "experts", technologists, and HN users since the AI bubble began. It feels like nobody has bothered to develop even a rudimentary understanding of statistical learning; even people who work in the field have a questionable understanding.

The fact that everyone's surprised every time a statistical model TRAINED ENTIRELY ON HUMAN GENERATED DATA (including all the junk, bias, propaganda, lies, and disinformation) acts and mimics human behavior, including our worst traits — then considers this evidence that they are intelligent — should be setting off alarm bells for everyone. Nothing about their actions should be surprising beyond the glaring ignorance of our entire species. The phrase "I am far too stupid to be this much smarter than average" is a recurring theme.

Now we are letting these mimics loose in meatspace by integrating them into physical robots, that will develop themselves, and manufacture themselves... and you realize that the terminator timeline is actually a cautionary tale of MIC incompetence, and we don't need to achieve anything near AGI or super-intelligence to annihilate our entire civilization or all life on earth.

children.author: jacquesm
children.textRawHtml:
Let's do a little experiment. I make a device. We'll call it 'H'. H is a little box. It has my name on it as the creator and a single ethernet port.

We connect H to the nearest network connection and wait for a bit to see what will happen. But because H is just a box there is no outward sign of it doing anything. Meanwhile H is hacking other people's properties left right and center.

If you didn't know that the technology in the box was LLM based would you still consider the box to have gone rogue or would you say that I had created a device with the intent of doing harm?

Because - to me at least - there is no difference. I don't care what is in the box, all I care about is the outcome of deploying a box which you know has the potential to start hacking stuff. It is entirely on me: (1) as the creator of a weapons grade hacking device and (2) as the person deploying such a device (3) as the person who is negligent in ensuring that the device does not harm others (4) as the person continuining the development of such a device after its potential to do harm is known to make sure it does not go out of control. I should be 100% liable for deploying this device with my name on it.

Intent is one angle here, they may not have intended for this to happen, and you'd hope so (though you can't even be 100% sure about that). But the negligence factor here is at least as large, if you know that you are making dangerous stuff the onus is on you to keep it secured. The power and the nature of the models is entirely secondary to the degree to which the purveyors of these models are losing control of their own creations.

Meanwhile, the models that they are warning us against are fairly well behaved and seem to be far less dangerous. But of course for those models that those naughty Chinese distilled from their we need regulation. How they manage to keep all this cognitively dissonant material in their heads is a mystery to me.
children.textZhHtml:
让我们做一个小实验。我制作一个设备。我们将其称为“H”。 H是一个小盒子。它上面有我作为创建者的名字和一个以太网端口。

我们将 H 连接到最近的网络连接，稍等一下看看会发生什么。但因为 H 只是一个盒子，所以没有任何外在迹象表明它在做任何事情。与此同时，H 正在黑客攻击其他人的财产。

如果你不知道盒子里的技术是基于 LLM 的，你还会认为这个盒子已经失控，还是会说我创造了一个旨在造成伤害的设备？

因为 - 至少对我来说 - 没有区别。我不在乎盒子里有什么，我只关心部署一个你知道有可能开始黑客攻击的盒子的结果。这完全取决于我：(1) 作为武器级黑客设备的创建者，(2) 作为部署此类设备的人，(3) 作为疏忽确保该设备不会伤害他人的人，(4) 作为在已知其潜在危害性后继续开发此类设备的人，以确保其不会失控。我应该对部署带有我名字的设备承担 100% 的责任。

这里的意图是一个角度，他们可能并没有打算让这种情况发生，而你也希望如此（尽管你甚至不能 100% 确定这一点）。但这里的疏忽因素至少同样大，如果你知道你正在制造危险的东西，你就有责任保证它的安全。模型的力量和本质完全取决于这些模型的提供者对自己的创造物失去控制的程度。

与此同时，他们警告我们反对的模型表现得相当好，而且似乎危险性要小得多。但当然，对于那些顽皮的中国人提炼出来的模型，我们需要监管。他们如何设法将所有这些认知上不和谐的材料保留在脑海中对我来说是一个谜。

I don't know enough to argue about whether passkeys are a trap or not, but I do know as a user that they appear to be a confusing mess.

When a website prompts me to set up a passkey, depending on the device I happen to be using at the time it could end up going to Google password manager, Samsung password manager, iCloud Keychain, or Windows somethingorother.

What happens when I go to the same site on a different platform? What if I can't use cross-device authentication because I'm on a locked-down work machine or one that simply doesn't have bluetooth? What if I want to consolidate them all in one platform just for the sake of being organised? What if I lose or simply don't have the device with a certain passkey near me?

I don't have the time or patience to work out any of that, which might absolutely be a 'me' problem, but TOTPs are pretty sodding frictionless in comparison. Scan QR in my chosen manager; type number into website; done. Why are passkeys better?

当网站提示我设置万能钥匙时，根据我当时使用的设备，它最终可能会转到 Google 密码管理器、三星密码管理器、iCloud 钥匙串或 Windows 等。

当我在不同的网站上访问同一网站时会发生什么情况平台？如果我因为使用​​的是锁定的工作计算机或根本没有蓝牙而无法使用跨设备身份验证怎么办？如果我只是为了组织起来而想将它们全部整合到一个平台上怎么办？如果我丢失了或者根本没有带有特定密钥的设备在我身边怎么办？

我没有时间或耐心来解决这些问题，这绝对是“我”的问题，但相比之下，TOTP 非常无摩擦。扫描我选择的经理中的二维码；在网站中输入号码；完毕。为什么密钥更好？

I thought "Passkeys are a trap" was going to be about this usability nightmare. Some sites, once connected via passkey, make it all but impossible to connect in another way. Some support multiple passkeys. Some do not. Some support passkey or something else. Some do not.

The idea and protocol are pretty solid, though we're back to a "biometrics as password" problem in many device flows, but every time I'm urged by a site to convert to a passkey, I wonder "is this site the sort that would screw this up?"

So far, it's about 30% of sites screwing it up...

children.author: vel0city
children.textRawHtml:
I've used a number of password managers over decades. I'm still having to copy and paste passwords from time to time due to poor/hostile website designs, needing to authenticate into a browser/app that doesn't have the plugin configured yet, bugginess on the plugin detecting the right site, etc. And in the end, if the user can copy and paste that wherever, the user will copy and paste that wherever.

Meanwhile there are other security benefits as well. With a password, that static credential is transmitted in the handshake. It can be mishandled somewhere in between, and now that entire root credential is potentially compromised. This is just impossible with a passkey. The credential never leaves the client. In some implementations, the credential never leaves a secure enclave, never even entering the client's system memory. You can't say the same for passwords, not even close.
children.textZhHtml:
几十年来我使用过许多密码管理器。由于糟糕/恶意的网站设计，需要对尚未配置插件的浏览器/应用程序进行身份验证，检测正确站点的插件存在错误等，我仍然不得不时不时地复制和粘贴密码。最后，如果用户可以将其复制并粘贴到任何地方，那么用户将将其复制并粘贴到任何地方。

同时还有其他安全优势。使用密码时，该静态凭证将在握手中传输。它可能会在两者之间的某个地方处理不当，现在整个根凭证可能会受到损害。这对于密钥来说是不可能的。凭证永远不会离开客户。在一些实现中，凭证永远不会离开安全飞地，甚至永远不会进入客户端的系统内存。对于密码，你不能说同样的话，甚至不是很接近。

LLMs have also pushed me to learn a lot, but I don’t find the shape to be terribly different than before. I rarely remember the exact sequence of commands or flags or syntax. What my learning was useful for before and after LLMs is to 1) build an intuition of how something behaves and what it should do and 2) expose me to non-obvious possibilities that I wouldn’t have come to on my own. With those two things in place, the next execution without the LLM is a docs search, same as it always was (for me maybe some people are better at remembering this stuff).

stories.title: The United Kingdom generates less electricity per person than in the 1970s
stories.titleZh: 英国人均发电量低于 20 世纪 70 年代

comments.author: andyjohnson0
comments.textRawHtml:
There's lots of amusingly Telegraph-esque outrage being posted here. But the article makes it clear that the reduction is due to reduction in demand, due in part to welcome improvements in efficiency, but also regrettable deindustrialization, and (neutral?) increased importing of electricity. Nobody is planning to ration electricity suppies.

I also wonder what the contribution of domestic solar and on-site industrial generation is? I'm a dev in a large manufacturing business and two of our three factory buildings are now covered in solar cells which power a lot of our operations. Some big industrial sites have on-site wind-powered generation too. Is that counted as generation in these stats? Or is it just manifested as reduced demand?

(Edit: added "being posted", "welcome" and "(neutral?)" for clarity)
comments.textZhHtml:
这里发布了许多有趣的《电报》式的愤怒。但文章明确指出，减少的原因是需求减少，部分原因是效率的提高，但也令人遗憾的是去工业化和（中性？）电力进口的增加。没有人计划定量供电。

我还想知道家庭太阳能和现场工业发电的贡献是什么？我是一家大型制造企业的开发人员，我们的三栋厂房中的两栋现在都覆盖了太阳能电池，为我们的大部分运营提供动力。一些大型工业场地也有现场风力发电。在这些统计数据中，这算作一代吗？或者只是表现为需求减少？

（编辑：为清楚起见添加了“正在发布”、“欢迎”和“（中立？）”）

children.author: roenxi
children.textRawHtml:
> Nobody is planning to ration electricity suppies.

If I search for "retail electricity price trends uk" I'm starting to see reports coming out of the UK like "UK electricity prices are now among the highest in the developed world." and "Household electricity prices have risen by almost 150% since 2010, and business electricity prices by nearly 175%" [0]. And now we see things like they've dropped below their 1970s per capita consumption.

That looks like rationing. Economies ration by raising prices until poor people can't consume as much. It doesn't sound like an efficiency gain. Mathematically speaking efficiency gains should actually involve people using more electricity [1] because there if it was worth spending that much money for X stuff now it makes even more sense because you can get >X stuff. It looks like they don't have enough energy and people are getting squeezed. I'd expect to see political instability in such an environment but the last time I checked only one of the major parties seemed to be in the process of collapsing (down from 2 in April) so they are doing better than expected on that front; I would expect riots in the streets with these sort of trends.

[0] https://ifs.org.uk/publications/electricity-prices

[1] https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jevons_paradox
children.textZhHtml:
> 没有人计划配给电力供应。

如果我搜索“英国零售电价趋势”，我开始看到来自英国的报告，例如“英国电价现在是发达国家中最高的电价之一”。 “自2010年以来，家庭电价上涨了近150%，商业电价上涨了近175%”[0]。现在我们看到他们的人均消费量已降至 20 世纪 70 年代以下。

这看起来像是配给。经济通过提高价格来进行配给，直到穷人无法消费那么多为止。这听起来不像是效率提升。从数学上讲，效率的提高实际上应该让人们使用更多的电力[1]，因为如果现在值得花那么多钱买 X 种东西，那么现在就更有意义了，因为你可以获得 >X 种东西。看起来他们没有足够的能量，人们正在受到挤压。我预计在这样的环境中会出现政治不稳定，但上次我检查时，只有一个主要政党似乎正处于崩溃的过程中（比 4 月份的 2 个有所下降），所以他们在这方面的表现比预期要好；我预计这种趋势会在街头发生骚乱。

[0] https://ifs.org.uk/publications/electricity-prices

[1] https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jevons_paradox

children.author: Dylan16807
children.textRawHtml:
> Mathematically speaking efficiency gains should actually involve people using more electricity [1] because there if it was worth spending that much money for X stuff now it makes even more sense because you can get >X stuff.

Light bulbs got 6x as efficient and roughly nobody wants 6x as much light.

Most appliances don't see much increased use from efficiency. And air conditioners have had pretty stable efficiency; other factors drive use changes there.
children.textZhHtml:
> 从数学上讲，效率的提高实际上应该涉及人们使用更多的电力 [1]，因为如果值得花那么多钱买 X 种东西，那么现在就更有意义了，因为你可以获得 >X 种东西。

灯泡的效率提高了 6 倍，而且大约没有人想要 6 倍的光。

大多数电器的效率并没有增加太多。 而且空调的效率也相当稳定；其他因素推动了那里的使用变化。

children.author: adrian_b
children.textRawHtml:
Actually even 8x as efficient.

An old 100 W incandescent bulb produced about 1500 lumens, and now a LED bulb of 12 or 13 W can produce slightly more than that.

In the now distant past, I used only 100 W incandescent bulbs, all of which had been replaced more than a decade ago with 13 W LED bulbs, so I have benefited from this 8x reduction in energy consumption.

The other significant reduction in electrical energy consumption happened when I replaced a many-decades-old refrigerator with a modern high-efficiency refrigerator.

Compared with a half century ago when I was a child, now I consume additional electrical energy with some computers, one or two of which are almost always on, and with a microwave oven used for cooking, but the additional energy consumption is normally less than what is saved by modern lighting and refrigeration technologies.
children.textZhHtml:
实际上效率甚至提高了 8 倍。

旧的 100 W 白炽灯泡可产生约 1500 流明，而现在 12 或 13 W LED 灯泡可产生略多的流明。

在遥远的过去，我只使用 100 W 白炽灯泡，所有这些灯泡在十多年前都已被 13 W LED 灯泡取代，所以我能源消耗减少了 8 倍。

电能消耗的另一个显着减少是当我用现代化的高效冰箱更换了几十年前的冰箱时。

与半个世纪前我还是个孩子的时候相比，现在我使用一些计算机（其中一两台几乎一直处于打开状态）以及用于烹饪的微波炉消耗了额外的电能，但额外的能耗通常少于现代照明和制冷所节省的电能技术。

children.author: xyzzy123
children.textRawHtml: What I don't get though is that with increased household efficiency and presumably an increase in population (i.e, density which usually lowers cost), and the benefits of efficiency improvements to generation and distribution... why is household energy spending is UP, even accounting for inflation?
children.textZhHtml: 我不明白的是，随着家庭效率的提高和人口的增加（即通常会降低成本的密度），以及发电和配电效率提高的好处......为什么家庭能源支出会增加，甚至考虑到通货膨胀？

children.author: epistasis
children.textRawHtml:
In the US, it's due to the cost of the grid, the part of the utility bill that PUCs allow utilities to charge a fixed rate of profit. So if utilities take 20% on that grid "maintenance" project, the utility drives up the price as high as possible.

This is why distributed solar is actually cheaper than utility scale solar all-in: you need less of that very very expensive grid, even if you pay 3x on the initial install costs.
children.textZhHtml:
在美国，由于电网成本（公用事业账单的一部分），公用事业公司允许公用事业公司收取固定的利润率。因此，如果公用事业公司在该电网“维护”项目上承担 20% 的费用，则公用事业公司会尽可能提高价格。

这就是为什么分布式太阳能实际上比公用事业规模太阳能全包更便宜的原因：即使您支付 3 倍的初始安装成本，您也需要更少的非常昂贵的电网。

children.author: andyjohnson0
children.textRawHtml:
In 1970 the UK domestic electricity grid and generating plants had been state owned since 1948, and was basically run by civil servants. This lasted until 1990-91 when it was all privatised by the Thatcher and Major governments (both Conservative).

Now in 2026 the main generators are EDF (French state owned), RWE (German), and Scottish Power (Spanish owned). These companies tend not to publish executive pay, but back in 2012 the CEO of EDF in the UK was being paid £1.2 million a year.

I would submit that all this has some bearing on why the prices have gone up.
children.textZhHtml:
1970年，英国国内电网和发电厂自1948年起一直为国有，基本上由公务员管理。这种情况一直持续到 1990-91 年，当时它被撒切尔夫人和主要政府（均为保守党）全部私有化。

现在到 2026 年，主要发电商是 EDF（法国国有）、RWE（德国）和 Scottish Power（西班牙拥有）。这些公司往往不公布高管薪酬，但早在 2012 年，英国 EDF 首席执行官的年薪就达到 120 万英镑。

我认为，所有这些都与价格上涨的原因有关。

children.author: reorder9695
children.textRawHtml: On the other hand more stoves are electric now rather than gas, new builds frequently have air source heating where they would've had gas or oil boilers, more cars are electric; all of which are huge percentages of a household's total energy consumption compared to something like lighting.
children.textZhHtml: 另一方面，现在更多的炉灶是电动的而不是燃气的，新建的建筑经常在原本有燃气或燃油锅炉的地方配备空气源加热，更多的汽车是电动的；与照明等能源消耗相比，所有这些都占家庭总能源消耗的很大一部分。

Not necessarily. In the bad old days folks would draw a continuous kW or more in the evenings just for lighting. 8kWh for an evening of lighting, or 1kWh for dinner, and 1kWh for lighting.

As for gas or oil boilers - oil is uncommon except in rural areas - gas is far more common but not as ubiquitous in the past as you’d think - many folks heated their homes with resistive electric radiators or IR heaters - so a heat pump is a huge efficiency win.
children.textZhHtml:
不一定。在过去糟糕的日子里，人们会在晚上连续消耗或更多的电力只是为了照明。晚上照明 8 千瓦时，晚餐 1 千瓦时，照明 1 千瓦时。

children.author: throwthrowuknow
children.textRawHtml: Somehow you’ve missed the drastic intensification of street, parking and building lighting at night not to mention headlights. People also seem much less concerned with leaving lights on in unused spaces as well.
children.textZhHtml: 不知何故，您错过了夜间街道、停车场和建筑照明的急剧增强，更不用说车头灯了。人们似乎也不太关心在未使用的空间里开灯。

children.textRawHtml: Street lighting already had very efficient bulbs so I think that's caused by other factors.  And headlights seem like other factors too.  Building lighting I'm not sure but that's more like a doubling.

children.author: noir_lord
children.textRawHtml:
> a very significant increase in the number and intensity of outdoor lights

I think the number of lights is about the same at least where I live in the UK, the big change is the light is now bright white not the yellow of the older sodium vapour lights.

I kinda miss that but mostly because it wasn't as bright and is what I grew up with, you can't really argue that the white light isn't more effective at it's primary goal (illumination) though.
children.textZhHtml:
> 户外灯的数量和强度显着增加

我认为至少在我居住的英国，灯的数量大致相同，最大的变化是灯现在是明亮的白色，而不是旧钠蒸气灯的黄色。

我有点怀念这一点，但主要是因为它没有那么亮，而且是我长大的，你不能真正说白光在其主要目标上不是更有效（照明）不过。

children.author: bluGill
children.textRawHtml:
> you can't really argue that the white light isn't more effective at it's primary goal (illumination) though.

IN fact white light is MUCH MUCH less effective. Red light doesn't affect your night vision, and yellow isn't much behind. White light means you can see very well where the light it, but you can't see beyond that radius and so more light is needed. I don't need to see colors at night (where white it good), I just need to see the dangers in time to avoid them, and so white is much worse for the goal.

Just to make it worse, it takes nearly an hour for your eyes to fully adjust to dark after leaving white light. So if the lights go off or you have to leave the place where they are shining you can't see as well.

White light is only good when you have enough of it that everything you want to see for the next hour is fully illuminated. If there is any exception to that, then you shouldn't have white lite.
children.textZhHtml:
> 不过，您不能真正认为白光在其主要目标（照明）方面并不更有效。

事实上，白光的效果要差得多。 红光不会影响你的夜视能力，黄光也不会影响你的夜视能力。 白光意味着您可以清楚地看到光所在的位置，但您无法看到超出该半径的区域，因此需要更多的光。我不需要在晚上看到颜色（白色很好），我只需要及时看到危险并避免它们，因此白色对于目标来说要差得多。

更糟糕的是，离开白光后，你的眼睛需要近一个小时才能完全适应黑暗。 因此，如果灯光熄灭或者您必须离开灯光照射的地方，您也将看不到东西。

只有当您有足够的白光以确保下一小时内您想看到的所有物体都被完全照亮时，白光才有用。 如果有任何例外，那么您不应该使用白色精简版。

children.author: avhception
children.textRawHtml:
It's the same here in Germany, and I very much dislike this development. We used to get so much beautiful fireflies in the summer here. Now they're mostly gone, and that's probably only the most visible damage.

Very appropriate nickname!
children.textZhHtml:
德国也是如此，我非常不喜欢这种发展。以前夏天我们这里有很多美丽的萤火虫。现在它们大部分都消失了，这可能只是最明显的损坏。

非常合适的昵称！

children.author: dghlsakjg
children.textRawHtml: The disappearance of fireflies is not related to lighting. That’s a global phenomena involving the mass collapse of insect populations.
children.textZhHtml: 萤火虫的消失与照明无关。这是一种涉及昆虫种群大规模崩溃的全球现象。

children.author: adrian_b
children.textRawHtml:
True, but besides insecticides and habitat destruction it is possible that the strong nocturnal lighting, which disorients insects, has contributed to this. Wherever insects are abundant, a strong white lamp at night will accumulate quickly dead insects around it.

Where I live, in Europe, when I was a child there was a great abundance of insects of many different kinds. If I did a walk around my home I could see insects from perhaps at least 10 different orders.

Nowadays, the only insects that are still abundant are the true bugs (Hemiptera) why all others have mostly disappeared (a few, like mosquitoes, may still be seen from time to time). I do not know the reason, but I assume that the true bugs might be more resistant to insecticides.
children.textZhHtml:
确实如此，但除了杀虫剂和栖息地破坏之外，强烈的夜间照明也可能导致昆虫迷失方向。凡是昆虫多的地方，晚上一盏强烈的白灯就会在周围迅速积聚死去的昆虫。

我住在欧洲，当我还是个孩子的时候，那里有大量不同种类的昆虫。如果我在家里散步，我可能会看到至少 10 种不同目的昆虫。

如今，唯一仍然丰富的昆虫是真正的昆虫（半翅目），因此所有其他昆虫大多都消失了（少数昆虫，如蚊子，可能仍会时不时地出现）。我不知道原因，但我认为真正的虫子可能对杀虫剂具有更强的抵抗力。
